strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: predicting answer failure before generation. The distinction between prediction and post-hoc detection is clear, and a lightweight probe over frozen question representations offers a practical approach.

Experiments cover four LLMs and three QA datasets, with comparisons against attention probes, prompting, entity-based methods, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. Table 1 supports the narrower empirical claim that question representations predict the constructed QA-success labels effectively and often match or outperform more expensive methods.

The reported transfer results are substantial. For example, LLaMA2-to-Mistral transfer on PopQA improves from 0.673 to 0.863 AUC after adaptation, approaching the target-specific probe's 0.874. The question-aligned minibatch ablation provides useful evidence about the proposed training strategy.

The efficiency evaluation separately reports feature-extraction costs and prediction latency. On LLaMA2–PopQA, FacLens takes 0.016 seconds per prediction versus 0.037 for SAT Probe. The appendices provide useful dataset filters, architecture specifications, optimizer settings, and baseline configurations.
weaknesses: The target-label-free evaluation protocol needs clarification before a clear Findings recommendation is warranted. Appendix D does not specify how adaptation checkpoints and training duration are selected without target labels, while Figures 7 and 9 show target-test AUC curves and motivate training/kernel choices. State the selection rule, distinguish exploratory experiments from final evaluation, and document synchronized question splits, exact generation prompts, and seeds. No implementation or processed-data release is identified in the manuscript.

Section 4.2 does not establish its central claim of similar conditional distributions across LLMs. A pooled classifier can infer model identity from distinct representation distributions and learn different decision functions while matching individually trained classifiers. Comparable AUC also does not imply comparable conditional probabilities. Prediction agreement on each domain and t-SNE of supervised features do not resolve this issue. The inference following Equation 4 should be revised; successful adaptation supports empirical transferability without establishing the claimed absence of concept shift.

The claimed 97% label accuracy is insufficiently supported. Footnote 2 audits only 20 negative, substring-matching examples per dataset and assumes every positive label is correct. An answer can convey the correct fact through an unlisted alias or paraphrase without containing a gold substring. Conversely, a matching string can appear in an incorrect statement. Both classes require auditing. The explicitly broad definition also includes refusals, so conclusions should remain scoped to short-answer QA failure rather than general response factuality.

The transfer comparison lacks a particularly relevant simple baseline: train a probe on target-model representations using the source model's labels for the same questions. This uses the same available supervision and could exploit correlated question difficulty without MMD. Applying source-model prediction scores directly to target-model labels would also be informative. Comparing primarily against direct application across incompatible representation spaces does not sufficiently isolate the value of the adaptation method.

Statistical uncertainty is not reported. Several improvements over strong baselines are below one AUC point, yet there are no confidence intervals or repeated-seed results. This particularly matters for NQ, which contains only 1,244 questions before splitting. Since PopQA and Entity Questions are template-based, evaluation on held-out entities or relations would also help assess whether the learned signal extends beyond recurring dataset regularities.

The human evaluation provides limited evidence of practical reliability. The 680 queries come from 22 volunteers who see the system's prediction before rating it, with no reported independent factual verification, comparison baseline, or class distribution. The 71% user-rated correctness therefore remains difficult to interpret. Calibration and accuracy-versus-abstention results would better support the probability estimates and three-way decisions presented by the demo.
